vaccines.why: Provides passive protection against severe RSV in infants and certain toddlers. RSV causes respiratory infections that can lead to bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and hospitalization, especially dangerous for premature infants and those with underlying health conditions.

recommendations.label: Infant — first RSV season (depends on maternal vaccination)

rules: Administer shortly before start of RSV season (Oct–Mar in most of continental U.S.)
If maternal RSV vaccine given ≥14 days before delivery, infant dose generally not needed; may consider in rare circumstances.

citations: file:child-schedule: RSV nirsevimab first-season timing and maternal status

recommendations.label: Second RSV season — high-risk or AI/AN

rules: Administer shortly before second RSV season.
If undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass for cardiac surgery, give an additional dose post-op.

citations: file:child-schedule: RSV second-season indications & timing

vaccines.why: Prevents chronic liver infection, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Hepatitis B is a serious liver disease that can cause lifelong infection, leading to liver failure, liver cancer, and death. The virus spreads through blood and body fluids, making it a significant public health concern.

recommendations.label: Routine infant series

rules: Use monovalent HepB for doses before 6 weeks of age.

branches.series: 4-dose (birth monovalent, then combination vaccine at 2, 4, 6 months)
rules: Combination HepB-containing vaccines are not used before 6 weeks of age.

vaccines.why: Prevents severe diarrhea, dehydration, and hospitalization in infants. Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe diarrhea in young children worldwide, causing millions of hospitalizations and deaths annually. The vaccine significantly reduces the risk of severe gastroenteritis and its complications.

recommendations.label: Routine infant oral series
citations: file:child-schedule: RV products, max age first dose 14w6d; final dose by 8m0d

vaccines.immunizingAgent: Diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis vaccine
vaccines.why: Prevents diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis; pertussis is severe in infants. Diphtheria causes severe throat infections and heart damage, tetanus leads to painful muscle spasms and death, while pertussis (whooping cough) causes severe coughing fits that can be fatal in infants and lead to pneumonia and brain damage.

recommendations.label: Routine 5-dose childhood series

rules: Prospective: may give at 12 months if ≥24 weeks since dose 3.
Dose 5 not needed if dose 4 given at ≥48 months AND ≥24 weeks after dose 3.

citations: file:child-schedule: DTaP routine series and dose-5 rule

vaccines.why: Prevents invasive Hib disease (meningitis, pneumonia). Haemophilus influenzae type b was once the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in children under 5, causing severe brain damage, hearing loss, and death. The vaccine has dramatically reduced these devastating infections.

recommendations.label: Routine infant/toddler series + booster

rules: Vaxelis is not recommended for the booster dose.

citations: file:child-schedule: Hib product-specific series and booster

vaccines.why: Prevents pneumococcal pneumonia, meningitis, and bacteremia. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes serious infections including pneumonia, blood infections, and meningitis. These diseases can lead to hospitalization, long-term complications like hearing loss and brain damage, and death, especially in young children and older adults.

recommendations.label: Routine infant series
citations: file:child-schedule: PCV routine series

vaccines.why: Prevents paralytic polio. Poliovirus can cause permanent paralysis, difficulty breathing, and death. While polio has been eliminated in most countries, vaccination remains crucial to prevent outbreaks and protect against imported cases. The disease can cause lifelong disability and requires intensive medical care.

recommendations.label: Routine childhood series

rules: Final dose at ≥48 months AND ≥24 weeks after previous dose.

citations: file:child-schedule: IPV routine series and final-dose rule

vaccines.why: Reduces risk of severe disease and hospitalization; schedules vary by manufacturer, age, and immune status. COVID-19 can cause severe respiratory illness, blood clots, heart problems, and long-term symptoms. Vaccination significantly reduces the risk of severe disease, hospitalization, and death, while also helping to prevent long COVID complications.

recommendations.label: Ages 6 months–17 years (not immunocompromised) — SCDM

schedule.series: Product- and age-specific per current season
rules: Ages 6 months–4 years: use same manufacturer for all doses within the series.
Follow current CDC COVID-19 schedule website for exact intervals and dose counts.

recommendations.label: Immunocompromised 6 months–18 years

schedule.series: Initial multi-dose series + additional dose at ~6 months; may need further doses per CDC clinical considerations
rules: Keep same manufacturer for initial series when required.
Consult clinical considerations for additional dosing.

citations: file:child-schedule: COVID-19 immunocompromised considerations

vaccines.why: Annual vaccination reduces hospitalization and protects vulnerable contacts. Influenza can cause severe respiratory illness, pneumonia, and death, especially in young children, older adults, and those with chronic conditions. Annual vaccination is necessary because flu viruses change each year, and it helps protect vulnerable populations through herd immunity.

recommendations.label: Annual vaccination (seasonal)

rules: Age 6 months–8 years: give 2 doses in a season if <2 lifetime prior doses before July 1, 2024; otherwise 1 dose.
Age ≥9 years: 1 dose.
LAIV not for close contacts of persons requiring a protected environment; if given, avoid contact/care for 7 days.

citations: file:child-schedule: Influenza annual rules incl. 2-dose algorithm and LAIV caveat

vaccines.why: Measles is highly contagious; mumps and rubella have serious complications. Measles can cause high fever, rash, pneumonia, brain inflammation, and death. Mumps can lead to painful swelling of salivary glands, meningitis, and infertility. Rubella during pregnancy can cause severe birth defects, miscarriage, or stillbirth. These diseases are highly preventable through vaccination.

recommendations.label: Routine 2-dose

rules: If MMRV used, minimum interval between doses is 12 weeks (3 months).
For infants 6–11 months traveling internationally: 1 early dose; then revaccinate with 2-dose series after 12 months.

citations: file:child-schedule: MMR routine + travel + MMRV interval

vaccines.why: Prevents chickenpox and complications (pneumonia, encephalitis). Chickenpox causes itchy rash, fever, and can lead to serious complications including bacterial skin infections, pneumonia, brain inflammation, and death. The virus can also reactivate later in life as shingles, causing severe nerve pain and rash. Vaccination prevents both chickenpox and reduces shingles risk.

recommendations.label: Routine 2-dose

rules: In catch-up, dose 2 valid if ≥4 weeks after dose 1 (≥13 years).

citations: file:child-schedule: Varicella routine and catch-up interval

vaccines.why: Prevents liver infection spread via contaminated food/water or close contact. Hepatitis A causes inflammation of the liver, leading to jaundice, fatigue, abdominal pain, and in severe cases, liver failure and death. The virus is highly contagious and can spread through contaminated food, water, or close personal contact. Vaccination provides long-term protection against this preventable disease.

recommendations.label: Routine 2-dose toddler
citations: file:child-schedule: HepA 12–23 months 2-dose ≥6 months apart

recommendations.label: Catch-up through 18 years
citations: file:child-schedule: HepA catch-up through 18y

vaccines.why: Protects against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis; adolescent booster reduces spread. Tetanus causes painful muscle spasms and can lead to death from respiratory failure. Diphtheria creates a thick coating in the throat that can block breathing and damage heart and nerves. Pertussis causes severe coughing that can break ribs and lead to pneumonia. The adolescent booster is crucial for protecting vulnerable infants.

recommendations.label: Adolescent booster
citations: file:child-schedule: Tdap 11–12y booster

recommendations.label: Catch-up 7–18 years

schedule.series: Use Tdap for first dose, then Td/Tdap per need
rules: If Tdap given at age 10y, adolescent booster at 11–12y is not needed.
If Tdap given at 7–9y, still give adolescent Tdap at 11–12y.

citations: file:child-schedule: Tdap catch-up and interval notes

recommendations.label: Pregnancy

rules: Give 1 dose during each pregnancy, preferably weeks 27–36.

citations: file:child-schedule: Tdap each pregnancy 27–36w

vaccines.why: Prevents HPV-related cancers; greatest benefit before exposure. Human papillomavirus causes nearly all cases of cervical cancer, as well as cancers of the throat, anus, penis, and vagina. HPV also causes genital warts. Vaccination before sexual activity provides the best protection, as it prevents infection with the most dangerous cancer-causing HPV types. This vaccine can prevent thousands of cancer cases annually.

recommendations.label: Routine/catch-up through 18 years

rules: If doses <5 months apart, give a 3rd dose ≥6 months after dose 1.
Also ensure 5 months between dose 1 and 3.

citations: file:child-schedule: HPV 2-dose vs 3-dose and immunocompromised

vaccines.why: Prevents rapidly progressive meningitis and bloodstream infection. Meningococcal disease can progress from mild symptoms to death within hours. It causes severe inflammation of the brain and spinal cord membranes, leading to brain damage, hearing loss, limb amputations, and death. The disease is particularly dangerous for adolescents and young adults, and vaccination provides crucial protection during this high-risk period.

recommendations.label: Routine adolescent series
citations: file:child-schedule: MenACWY routine 11–12 + 16 booster

recommendations.label: Catch-up 13–18 years

rules: Age 13–15: 1 dose now + booster at 16–18 (≥8 weeks).
Age 16–18: 1 dose.

citations: file:child-schedule: MenACWY catch-up rules

recommendations.label: High-risk indications (asplenia, HIV, complement deficiency/inhibitor use, travel to endemic areas)

rules: Menveo: 2–23 months schedules vary by starting age (2,4,6,12; or 3–6 months schedules; or 7–23 months 2-dose).
At ≥24 months: Menveo or MenQuadfi 2 doses ≥8 weeks apart.
Boosters per ongoing risk.

citations: file:child-schedule: MenACWY special situations + travel + product minimum ages

vaccines.why: Prevents serogroup B disease; shared clinical decision-making for healthy adolescents. Meningococcal B disease causes the same devastating effects as other meningococcal types - rapid progression to meningitis, bloodstream infection, and death. While less common than other serogroups, it's equally deadly and can cause permanent disabilities. The vaccine is recommended for adolescents and young adults who are at increased risk.

recommendations.label: SCDM (healthy 16–23 years)

rules: Use same brand for all doses. Penbraya option when co-admin with MenACWY same day (age ≥10y).

citations: file:child-schedule: MenB SCDM dosing, rapid option, Penbraya

recommendations.label: High-risk (asplenia, complement deficiency/inhibitor use) age ≥10 years

schedule.series: 3-dose (0, 1–2, 6 months) with brand consistency; boosters per risk
rules: If dose 2 ≥6 months after dose 1, dose 3 not needed.
If dose 3 <4 months after dose 2, add a 4th dose ≥4 months later.

citations: file:child-schedule: MenB special situations and booster logic

vaccines.why: Maternal vaccination during pregnancy protects newborns via transplacental antibodies. RSV is the leading cause of severe respiratory illness in infants. Maternal vaccination during pregnancy provides antibodies that cross the placenta to protect newborns during their first months of life when they're most vulnerable. This approach prevents severe RSV disease and reduces hospitalizations in the critical early months.

recommendations.label: Seasonal administration in pregnancy

rules: Administer during 32w0d–36w6d gestation in season (Sep–Jan in most of continental U.S.).
Do not repeat in subsequent pregnancies; use infant nirsevimab instead.

citations: file:child-schedule: Maternal RSV timing and subsequent-pregnancy rule

vaccines.why: Prevents dengue in seropositive children living in endemic U.S. territories. Dengue fever causes high fever, severe headache, joint pain, and in severe cases, dengue hemorrhagic fever which can lead to shock, bleeding, and death. The vaccine is specifically for children who have had a previous dengue infection and live in endemic areas, as it can prevent severe disease in subsequent infections.

recommendations.label: Residents in endemic areas with prior dengue infection

rules: Not for travelers; residents only in endemic areas listed by CDC.

citations: file:child-schedule: Dengue indications, endemic areas, 3-dose schedule

vaccines.why: Reduces mpox risk in persons with defined sexual exposure risks. Mpox (formerly monkeypox) causes painful skin lesions, fever, and swollen lymph nodes. While usually self-limiting, it can cause severe complications including secondary infections, scarring, and in rare cases, death. The vaccine provides protection for individuals at higher risk of exposure and helps prevent outbreaks in vulnerable populations.

recommendations.label: Risk-based (≥18 years)
citations: file:child-schedule: Mpox age ≥18 and risk criteria; 2-dose schedule
